procedural_history.originating_court: Disciplinary Committee of the Bar Council of India
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated October 26, 1969, of the Disciplinary Committee of the Bar Council of India in D.C. Appeal No. 18 of 1968, suspending the appellant from practice for a period of one year.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The text mentions a case from the High Court of Bombay where an advocate was found guilty of misconduct, but no disciplinary action was taken. An appeal by special leave was sought, but the Judicial Committee did not advise granting it, primarily because the High Court's decision was an exercise of statutory discretion.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The case reached the Supreme Court as a Civil Appeal No. 2259 of 1969, an appeal under Section 38 of the Advocate's Act, 1961. It was initially an appeal by special leave. A preliminary objection was raised by the respondent regarding the maintainability of the appeal, but this objection was rejected.

directions: The order of the Bar Council of India is set aside.
There shall be no order as to costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Advocate-General can be considered a 'person aggrieved' under Section 37 of the Advocates Act, 1961, and thus have the locus standi to file an appeal against an order of the disciplinary committee of a State Bar Council.

facts: A disciplinary committee of a State Bar Council initiated proceedings against an advocate and, after a hearing, found him not guilty of professional misconduct.
The Advocate-General of the State, who had been given notice of the proceedings as required by Section 35(2) of the Advocates Act and had appeared before the committee, disagreed with the decision.
The Advocate-General filed an appeal to the Bar Council of India under Section 37 of the Act.
The advocate raised a preliminary objection, arguing that the Advocate-General was not a "person aggrieved" and therefore had no right (locus standi) to file the appeal.
The Bar Council of India's disciplinary committee overruled the objection, heard the appeal, found the advocate guilty, and suspended him from practice for one year.
law: Section 37 of the Advocates Act, 1961, allows "any person aggrieved" by an order of a State Bar Council's disciplinary committee to prefer an appeal to the Bar Council of India.
Section 35(2) of the Act requires that the Advocate-General of the State be given notice of disciplinary proceedings and an opportunity to be heard.
The central legal question is the interpretation of the phrase "person aggrieved" and whether the Advocate-General, in his official capacity, falls within this category.
application: The Supreme Court (by majority) defined a "person aggrieved" as someone who has suffered a detriment, pecuniary or otherwise, or some form of prejudice from an order.
The Court reasoned that merely being given notice of a proceeding and the right to appear and make submissions does not automatically confer the status of an aggrieved person with a right to appeal.
The Court held that the Advocate-General's role under the Act is to assist the disciplinary committee. Once he has participated in the hearing, his duty is fulfilled.
The Advocate-General does not have a personal stake or grievance in the outcome. His disagreement with the committee's decision does not constitute a legal grievance or prejudice to him.

To be considered "aggrieved," the Advocate-General would need to show that the committee's error was something he had a specific duty to correct, a duty which the Court found was not cast upon him by the Act or general law in the context of an appeal.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded, by a majority, that the Advocate-General was not a 'person aggrieved' within the meaning of Section 37 of the Advocates Act, 1961. Therefore, the appeal filed by him before the Bar Council of India was incompetent.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Advocate-General can be considered a 'person aggrieved' under Section 37 of the Advocates Act, 1961, and thus have the locus standi to file an appeal against an order of the disciplinary committee of a State Bar Council.
appellant_arguments: The Advocate-General does not represent the public interest in these proceedings and therefore cannot be considered a 'person aggrieved' by the Disciplinary Committee's order.
The provision in Section 35 of the Act, which merely entitles the Advocate-General to receive a notice of the hearing, does not confer upon him the right to appeal as a 'person aggrieved'.
respondent_arguments: The Advocate-General has a statutory role in the proceedings, as evidenced by the requirement under Section 35(2) that he be given notice and an opportunity to be heard.

By virtue of his office and his duty to uphold the standards of the legal profession, the Advocate-General has sufficient interest in the outcome of disciplinary proceedings to be considered a 'person aggrieved' if he believes the committee's order is incorrect, thus giving him the right to appeal under Section 37.

cases.principle: For the general principle that the meaning of the expression 'person aggrieved' must be determined by the context of the specific statute in question, rather than by referencing its meaning in different statutes.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A legal grievance must be a tendency to injure the appellant. The belief that an order is wrong or that it acquits someone who ought to be convicted does not, by itself, give rise to a legal grievance. The expression conferring the right to appeal is to be construed as including the Advocate-General.
obiter: A decision in disciplinary matters is not a judgment of a court but is only deemed to be so by the legislature.
An undefined expression in a statute must be construed by reference to the context of the enactment in which it appears and all the circumstances.
The court's conclusion on the legal question does not reflect any opinion on the factual merits of the advocate's plea.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Advocate-General cannot be considered a 'person aggrieved' under Section 37 of the Advocates Act, 1961, and therefore lacks the locus standi to file an appeal against an order of a disciplinary committee. A mere disagreement with the committee's decision, or the belief that it is erroneous, constitutes a personal opinion and does not give rise to a legal grievance. The Advocate-General's role is not that of a 'guardian angel of the Bar' or a general champion of public interest; his functions are limited to those specified by statute, and the right to be heard in a proceeding does not automatically confer a right to appeal its outcome.
legal_tests_applied: To qualify as a 'person aggrieved', one must have a legal grievance, which must be a tendency to injure him.
The fact that an order is wrong or acquits someone who the appellant thinks ought to be convicted does not by itself give rise to a legal grievance.
A matter does not become one of public interest merely because the Advocate-General feels a decision is erroneous or would have arrived at a different conclusion.
why_appellant_lost: The Advocate-General's belief that the disciplinary committee's decision was wrong was considered merely his personal opinion, which is insufficient to make him a 'person aggrieved'.

The court rejected the argument that the Advocate-General represents the public interest in a general capacity, stating he is not the 'guardian angel of the Bar' or the 'champion of public interest in any matter save as specified in a statute'.
The Advocate-General's statutory right to be heard during the proceedings was deemed not to confer upon him an unqualified right to appeal the final decision.
why_respondent_won: The Advocate-General could not demonstrate that the disciplinary committee's order caused him a legal grievance with a tendency to injure him.
The Advocate-General is not a party to the disciplinary proceedings, and his statutory role is limited to appearing and making submissions, which does not grant him the locus standi to appeal.
The non-acceptance of the Advocate-General's views by the disciplinary committee does not, in itself, make him a person aggrieved.
policy_considerations: An Advocate-General in India is not the guardian angel of the Bar, nor is he the champion of public interest in any matter save as specified in a statute.

A decision by the disciplinary committee cannot necessarily be said to raise a point of public interest merely because the Advocate-General feels that it is erroneous or that he himself would have arrived at a different conclusion.
